green-revolution-s1.title: Wheat yields in two regions, 1950 to 2000

plot.label: Line chart of wheat yield in two invented regions, 1950 to 2000: Region X, an irrigated plain, rises from 0.8 to 2.8 tonnes per hectare, climbing fastest after 1960; Region Y, a dry region that relies on rain, rises slowly from 0.7 to 1.2.

green-revolution-s2.title: Four countries and the Green Revolution

map.label: Reference map of the world with four countries marked: A in South Asia, B in North America south of the United States, C in Southeast Asia and D in West Africa

items.q: Which statement compares the two regions in the chart?
options: Yields rose in both, but much faster in Region X after 1960
Yields rose quickly in Region Y after 1960 but fell in Region X
Yields were the same in both regions in 2000
Yields in both regions stayed flat from 1950 to 2000

why.correct: A compare speaks of both lines: both rise, but the irrigated plain pulls far ahead after 1960, when Green Revolution seeds spread.
options: Right: Region X climbs from 1.0 to 2.8 after 1960, while Region Y rises slowly to 1.2.
Region X rises steeply; Region Y rises slowly. Neither falls.
In 2000 Region X yields 2.8 and Region Y 1.2 tonnes per hectare.
Both lines rise, Region X much more steeply.

items.q: By what percent did wheat yield in Region X increase from 1960 to 1990?

mistakes.why: You divided the new value by the old one (2.5 / 1.0 × 100). Percent change uses the change: (2.5 - 1.0) / 1.0 × 100.
1.5 is the change in tonnes per hectare. Divide it by the 1960 value and multiply by 100 to get a percent.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the gap between the two regions after 1960?
options: Region Y planted the new seeds first, so its soil was worn out
Region X stopped irrigating after 1960 and switched to rain-fed crops
The new seeds needed water and fertilizer, which Region X could supply
GMO crops were planted in Region X in the 1960s

why.correct: The Green Revolution was a package: high-yield seeds plus irrigation, fertilizer and pesticides. Where water was short, yields rose much less.
options: If Region Y had planted them first, its line would rise first; it rises least.
The legend calls Region X an irrigated plain.
Right: high-yield varieties give big gains only with irrigation and fertilizer, which the irrigated plain had.
GMOs spread on farms from the late 1990s, not the 1960s.

items.q: A student uses Region X alone to argue that the Green Revolution ended hunger everywhere. Why is this conclusion weak?
options: Region X's yield fell after 1990
The chart shows no data before 1960
Region Y's yield rose faster than Region X's over the whole period
Region Y shows gains were small where water was scarce

why.correct: Results at one place do not show a global pattern. Regions without irrigation, such as much of Sub-Saharan Africa, gained far less.
options: Region X keeps rising, from 2.5 to 2.8.
It starts in 1950.
Region Y rose more slowly.
Right: the chart itself shows uneven results; one region cannot stand for the world.

items.q: In the 1950s, Norman Borlaug and other scientists bred short, disease-resistant wheat at a research center in one marked country. Which letter is it?
options: A
B
C
D

why.correct: Wheat breeding in Mexico from the 1940s and 1950s gave the seeds that South Asian farmers later adopted.
options: A marks India, which later planted the Mexican wheat widely from the mid-1960s.
Right: B marks Mexico, where the new wheat varieties were bred.
C marks the Philippines, where a rice institute bred the high-yield rice IR8.
D marks Niger, in the dry Sahel of West Africa.

items.q: In 1966 a research institute released IR8, a high-yield rice. In which marked country was it bred?
options: A
B
C
D

why.correct: IR8 came from the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines and spread across rice-growing Asia.
options: A marks India, a major adopter of the new rice and wheat.
B marks Mexico, where the wheat was bred.
Right: C marks the Philippines, home of the International Rice Research Institute.
D marks Niger, where rice is a minor crop.

items.q: Farmers in the country marked D gained much less from the Green Revolution than farmers in the country marked A. Which reason best explains the difference?
options: D farms dry, rain-fed land with little irrigation
D's farmers had no crops of their own until the 1970s
D is too far north for wheat and rice to grow
D adopted GMO crops instead in the 1960s

why.correct: The Green Revolution centered on wheat and rice with irrigation. Dry regions growing millet, sorghum and cassava, such as the Sahel, gained less.
options: Right: the new seeds were mainly wheat and rice and needed water, which much of Niger lacks.
Niger has been farmed for thousands of years; its farmers grow millet and sorghum.
Niger is closer to the equator than India; the limits are water and crop type, not latitude.
GMO crops did not spread on farms until the late 1990s.

items.q: About when did the Green Revolution spread across many less developed countries?
options: From the 1700s through the 1800s
From the 1960s through the 1980s
About 10,000 years ago
From the late 1990s onward

why.correct: The term was coined in 1968, and the main spread ran from the 1960s into the 1980s.
options: That was the Second Agricultural Revolution.
Right: the new seeds spread widely from the mid-1960s through the 1980s.
That was the First Agricultural Revolution.
GMO crops came into wide use from the late 1990s, after the Green Revolution.

items.q: What makes a high-yield variety different from the older local seeds it replaced?
options: Its genes were changed in a lab by inserting DNA from another species
It needs no fertilizer or water to grow well
It grows tall so its stalks can reach more sunlight
It grows more grain per hectare when given water and fertilizer

why.correct: High-yield varieties were bred by crossing plants, not by lab gene changes. Short, stiff stalks held heavier grain, and yields depended on water and fertilizer.
options: That describes a GMO. Green Revolution seeds came from careful cross-breeding.
It needs more of both to reach its high yields.
Many were bred short, so heavy heads of grain would not knock the stalks over.
Right: high-yield varieties were bred to turn water and fertilizer into more grain.

items.q: A news story calls GMO soybeans "part of the Green Revolution." Why is this incorrect?
options: GMOs came decades later, in the late 1990s
GMOs were grown long before the Green Revolution began
Soybeans were domesticated in the Fertile Crescent
The Green Revolution did not use any new seeds

why.correct: Keep the two apart: Green Revolution seeds were bred by crossing plants (1960s to 1980s); GMOs have genes changed in a lab and spread from the late 1990s.
options: Right: the Green Revolution used cross-bred seeds from the 1960s; lab gene changes spread on farms from the late 1990s.
GMOs came after the Green Revolution, not before.
Soybeans were domesticated in East Asia; in any case, this is not why the claim is wrong.
New high-yield seeds were at its center.

items.q: In Punjab, India, Green Revolution farms pump groundwater to irrigate rice and wheat. What negative environmental effect has this caused?
options: More forest cover as farmers leave the land
Less use of chemical fertilizer and pesticide on the fields
Falling water tables from pumping faster than rain refills
Wetter soils because rain increased in the region

why.correct: Irrigated rice and wheat need much water. Pumping more groundwater than rain replaces makes water tables fall, a cost of the package.
options: Punjab's land is intensively farmed, not returning to forest.
Green Revolution farming uses more fertilizer, not less.
Right: heavy pumping for thirsty crops has lowered groundwater levels in Punjab.
The problem comes from pumping, not from changes in rain.

items.q: Which was a negative social effect of the Green Revolution in parts of South Asia?
options: Grain prices rose because harvests became smaller
Farmers returned to shifting cultivation in the forests
Fewer people could buy rice and wheat in the market
Farmers who could not afford inputs fell behind or into debt

why.correct: The package favored farmers with land, water and credit. Inequality between farmers often grew even as total food supply rose.
options: Harvests grew, and grain prices generally fell.
Green Revolution farming is intensive and fixed.
More grain made rice and wheat more widely available.
Right: seeds, fertilizer, pumps and pesticides cost money, so larger farmers gained most and some small farmers borrowed heavily.

items.q: How does the Green Revolution challenge Malthusian theory?
options: It proved that population grows faster than food
Technology raised food output faster than population grew
It stopped population growth in South Asia
It showed that famines are caused by too few people

why.correct: Malthus (1798) argued food grows slowly. The Green Revolution raised yields so much that food per person rose in many countries. Neo-Malthusians reply that it depends on water and fuel that may run short.
options: That is Malthus's claim; the Green Revolution is evidence against it.
Right: Malthus expected food supply to grow slowly; new seeds and inputs made it grow quickly.
Population kept growing; food grew faster.
Malthus linked famines to too many people for the food; the Green Revolution showed food supply can rise.

items.q: Which were parts of the Green Revolution package? Select all that apply.
options: High-yield varieties of wheat and rice
Chemical fertilizer and irrigation
Genetically modified seeds made in a lab
The four-field rotation of Norfolk, England
Clearing new rainforest plots each few years

why.correct: High-yield seeds, fertilizer, irrigation, pesticides and machines made up the Green Revolution package.
options: Right: the core of the package.
Right: the new seeds needed both to reach high yields.
GMOs came in the late 1990s, after the Green Revolution.
That was part of the Second Agricultural Revolution in the 1700s.
That is shifting cultivation, an extensive system.

items.q: Put these big changes in farming in order, from earliest to most recent.
options: First domestication of crops in hearths
Crop rotation and machines in Britain
High-yield wheat and rice spread in Asia
GMO crops are sold to farmers

why.correct: The First Agricultural Revolution, the Second (1700s to 1800s), the Green Revolution (1960s to 1980s), then GMO crops (late 1990s).

items.q: Build an explanation of one effect of the Green Revolution in a named place.

why.correct: Place, technology and effect, joined by "so".

specific.frame: In ___, farmers planted ___ with irrigation and fertilizer, so ___.
specific.model: In Punjab, India, farmers planted high-yield varieties of wheat with irrigation and fertilizer, so wheat harvests rose sharply in the late 1960s and 1970s.

place.label: Place
options: Punjab, India
Iowa in the 1800s
many places

why.1: Iowa in the 1800s belongs to the Second Agricultural Revolution.
why.2: Name a real place; "many places" earns no credit.

concept.label: What they planted
options: high-yield varieties of wheat
GMO corn

why.1: GMO corn came in the late 1990s, after the Green Revolution.

effect.label: Effect
options: wheat harvests rose sharply in the late 1960s and 1970s
wheat harvests fell because the soil was too wet

why.1: Harvests rose; that was the point of the package.
